source.text: נוּגֵ֧י מִ/מּוֹעֵ֛ד אָסַ֖פְתִּי מִמֵּ֣/ךְ הָי֑וּ מַשְׂאֵ֥ת עָלֶ֖י/הָ חֶרְפָּֽה׃

translation.text: I have gathered[b] those grieving over the appointed festival[a]—they were from you; reproach was a burden upon her[c][d][e].

footnotes.text: Or 'those afflicted from the appointed assembly'; the Hebrew is difficult, and the phrase may refer either to people grieving because they are deprived of the festival or to those removed from the festal gathering.
Or 'I gathered' or, in prophetic context, 'I will gather.'
The pronoun 'her' likely refers to Zion/Jerusalem.

Or ‘I have gathered those grieving over the appointed festival from you; they were a reproach upon her, a burden.’ The Hebrew is compressed. The main reading follows the received accents in joining ‘from you’ with ‘they were’; its final ‘was’ is supplied, with past time inferred from context. The accents do not make the alternative impossible.

Selected Greek editions instead ask ‘Woe, who took reproach upon her?’ and join the festival phrase to the preceding verse. The published Murabbaʿat Hebrew transcription partly preserves the received sequence, with supplied and uncertain letters. Neither comparison establishes an exact lost Hebrew wording or historical priority.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The form is best taken as a substantive participial/adjectival expression describing people in a state of grief or affliction. 'Those grieving' preserves the personal reference and emotional force without over-specifying the cause.

lexical_decisions.lexicon: BDB printed p.387; GKC §130a; retained festival gloss
lexical_decisions.rationale: Align the chosen field with the already existing English ‘over’, not a new lexical preference. BDB's visually consulted page387 identifies נוּגֵי as a construct participle before a preposition; GKC§130a allows this construction. The festival/grief gloss remains a common comparison input, not newly certified. The causal/deprivation/removal alternatives in the existing note remain unresolved. No fresh HALOT consultation.

The qatal 1cs is formally past/perfect. In prophetic discourse it may function with future force, but here 'I have gathered' preserves the Hebrew form while remaining natural in English. The surrounding restoration context allows either a prophetic perfect or a simple perfective statement.

מִמֵּךְ has a 2fs suffix. Retain literal ‘from you’ while joining it with הָיוּ, supported by their munach/athnach grouping. Source or membership is possible; ‘belonged to you’ would select a further relation. Accents are later interpretive grouping, not original punctuation or an absolute syntactic veto. Attaching this phrase instead to ‘I have gathered’ remains a serious alternative. No fresh HALOT consultation.

Qatal3cp supplies the explicit ‘they were’ in ‘they were from you’. The final nominal clause has its own English-supplied ‘was’, with past time a contextual choice, not a second finite Hebrew verb. The older parse resumes the mourners as subjects of burden/reproach across athnach; poetic predication remains possible. No fresh HALOT consultation.

The pointed form is an absolute feminine noun, not construct מַשְׂאַת. BDB's visually consulted page673 associates the Zephaniah3:18 burden with reproach. Interpret ‘a burden upon her’ as a predicate preceding subject ‘reproach’; this is grammatical, not uniquely established. The alternative treats the people as a burden/reproach. Neither kindness to those people nor theological attractiveness decides syntax. No fresh HALOT consultation.

Align chosen wording with actual ‘upon her’; the 3fs suffix remains unchanged and likely refers to Zion/Jerusalem. Mercha links burden with this prepositional phrase, followed by tiphcha before reproach. This supports, but does not compel, the adopted nominal predicate. A switch from ‘you’ to ‘her’ does not establish different referents. No fresh HALOT consultation.

Render the absolute feminine noun as ‘reproach’, here the subject of a separate nominal clause: ‘reproach was a burden upon her’. This changes subject assignment, not the written or pointed source. The older personal subject with abstract predicates remains possible in poetic Hebrew. Copula and past time are supplied contextually, not certified by grammar alone. No fresh HALOT consultation.

theological_decisions.issue: Clause attachment and the burden of reproach
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: The gathered people were from Zion; reproach was a burden upon her.
alternative_readings: The LORD gathered grieving people from Zion; they were a reproach upon her, a burden.
theological_decisions.rationale: Prefer locally complete clauses supported by received grouping and available nominal syntax, without selecting by pastoral desirability. The alternative can describe the people's humiliating condition without morally condemning them. The feminine reference and supplied final copula remain interpretive; neither parse nor the versional differences establish historical priority.

value.text: I have gathered those grieving over the appointed festival from you[a]; they were a reproach upon her[c][b], a burden.

footnotes.text: Or 'those afflicted from the appointed assembly'; the Hebrew is difficult, and the phrase may refer either to people grieving because they are deprived of the festival or to those removed from the festal gathering.
Or 'I gathered' or, in prophetic context, 'I will gather.'

value.rationale: The form is best taken as a substantive participial/adjectival expression describing people in a state of grief or affliction. 'Those grieving' preserves the personal reference and emotional force without over-specifying the cause.

מוֹעֵד commonly denotes an appointed time or festival assembly in cultic contexts. In this context of Zion's restoration, the sense likely concerns grief connected with the loss of festal gathering. 'Because of the appointed festival' captures the causal nuance often recognized here, though the Hebrew preposition can be understood in more than one way.

The qatal 1cs is formally past/perfect. In prophetic discourse it may function with future force, but here 'I have gathered' preserves the Hebrew form while remaining natural in English. The surrounding restoration context allows either a prophetic perfect or a simple perfective statement.
The 2fs suffix refers to the feminine addressee, likely Zion/Jerusalem. 'From you' is the most direct rendering and leaves the relational nuance intact.
Simple copular past fits the clause naturally and reflects the Hebrew verb without expansion.
Here the noun is best understood in the sense of a load or burden, not 'oracle.' The context is social disgrace borne in relation to Zion/her people.
The preposition על with 3fs suffix is rendered straightforwardly. 'On her' works idiomatically with 'burden' and preserves the feminine referent, likely Zion.
חרפה regularly denotes reproach, disgrace, or shame. 'Reproach' preserves both the social and verbal dimensions of public dishonor.

value.issue: Syntactic ambiguity of the verse and referents
value.chosen_reading: The verse speaks of the LORD gathering people from Zion who grieve over the loss of the appointed festival; these people had been a burden of reproach upon her.
alternative_readings: The verse speaks of removing from Zion the reproach associated with those excluded from the festival.
The final clause may be rendered more appositionally: 'the reproach upon her was a burden for them.'
value.rationale: The Hebrew is notably compressed and difficult. The chosen rendering preserves the main verbal action ('I have gathered') and keeps the final clause close to the Masoretic wording without importing a stronger interpretive paraphrase than necessary. This maintains the restoration theme while respecting the text's ambiguity.
